title: The case for direct placement in a competitive hiring market.
summary: Learn when direct placement is the right hiring model, what a slow search costs, and what to look for in a recruiting partner.
body_markdown:
### Key takeaways:


- Direct placement is the right fit when the role is permanent, the candidate has room to grow, and culture alignment is part of the evaluation from the first interview.
- Hire for trajectory. Someone who can do 60% of the job today and learn the other 40% will stay longer than someone who can do all of it on day one.
- AI-driven auto-apply tools have increased resume volume roughly 10x while dropping the applicant-to-hire conversion rate to 0.5%, making speed and verification more important than ever.
- A role open for 90 days can cost thousands in direct expenses before factoring in team burnout, cultural damage, and cascading attrition.
- Look for a recruiting partner where the same person manages the client relationship and the candidate relationship, and where specialization shows up as network depth, not just subject-matter knowledge.


When a strong candidate hits the market, the window to hire them is narrow. SHRM research puts median time-to-fill at


[39 days for nonexecutive roles in 2026](https://www.shrm.org/in/topics-tools/research/recruiting-benchmarking/full-data-brief) , down from 44 in 2025. But that improvement hasn't kept pace with how quickly top talent moves. The best candidates are typically off the market


[within 10 days of becoming available](https://www.theresource.com/2025/10/13/average-time-to-hire/) . Meanwhile,


[57% of job seekers](https://treegarden.io/blog/average-time-to-hire-benchmarks-2026/) lose interest when a hiring process drags on. What feels internally like thoroughness reads externally like indecision, and candidates who have other options will take them.


I've spent 14 years in tech recruiting, working direct placement, contract, and consulting engagements across the United States. I run a full desk, so I'm the same person talking to the hiring leader and the candidate on every placement. I consistently see hiring leaders who know they need a permanent hire but keep adding friction to the process instead of removing it. A well-run direct placement search moves fast enough to reach the best candidates before they accept somewhere else.


## What direct placement is, and when it's the right call


In a direct placement engagement, a recruiter sources, screens, and presents candidates for a permanent role on the employer's payroll from day one. There's no contract period, and no trial phase. The company is committing to a full-time hire, and the search is built around finding someone who'll stay.


Not every open role warrants that commitment, and defaulting to direct placement without thinking it through tends to produce turnover that makes the next hire even harder. Here are the signs that a direct placement is the right move.


**The role is permanent and tied to long-term growth.** Direct placement makes sense when a company needs someone to own a function for the foreseeable future, or when it's building a


[leadership pipeline where internal promotion](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/what-is-internal-mobility) is part of the plan. Bringing someone in permanently gives them a reason to learn the business deeply, and it gives the company an easier path to promoting from within than pulling an outside candidate into a leadership role later.


**The right candidate has room to develop in the role.** Where I see companies misjudge direct placement is in how they scope the role. A strong candidate needs to handle the core functions of the job from day one. But if someone has nothing to learn from you, they'll perform well for a while, and then they'll leave. A smart employer builds skills into the role that the candidate can learn and grow into. I call it the six-out-of-10 rule: hire someone who can do 60% of the job today and who you trust to learn the other 40%. The engineers I can never recruit away from my clients are the ones whose companies hired for trajectory and gave them room to grow.


**Culture alignment carries as much weight as technical skills.** Interview time is shifting. I'm watching more of my clients move away from technical checklists and spend that time evaluating


[how a candidate will perform on the job](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/behavioral-interview-questions) : how they handle friction, take ownership, and fit within the team.


Nearly


[85% of new hires stayed past 90 days in 2025](https://www.hrdive.com/news/hiring-benchmarks-report-employ-2025-more-applicants/809604/) . That sounds like a strong number, but it’s down from 93.9% the year before. If you want a permanent hire to stick around, build culture alignment into the evaluation from the first interview.


## What slows direct placement down, and what it costs


AI has changed the speed and the mechanics of direct placement searches in ways that are working against most employers right now. Auto-apply tools have flooded the top of the funnel. AI has also made it easy to tailor a resume to any job description, so a candidate who isn’t qualified for the role can still look like a match on paper. The (Dis)honest Job Search survey found that


[79% of job seekers are now using AI tools in their applications](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/dishonest-job-search-survey-results) , and I'm hearing from clients who are seeing a roughly 10x increase in resume volume per posting. The


[applicant-to-hire conversion rate](https://www.pin.com/blog/sourcing-benchmarks-report/) across industries has dropped to about 0.5%, or one offer for every 200 applicants. That volume eats up days before a hiring leader ever talks to a real candidate, and once those conversations start, they're starting from a place of distrust. Hiring teams end up spending more time verifying whether candidates are who they say they are than evaluating whether they're the right fit.


That distrust runs in both directions. Candidates are scrutinizing recruiter outreach the same way hiring teams are scrutinizing resumes, and both sides have good reason for caution. The question for employers is how to structure a search that rebuilds that trust quickly enough to keep the best candidates engaged.


### The cost of a slow or failed search


That verification burden is adding time at every stage, and the cost adds up. I estimate that a role open for 90 days runs $12,000 to $30,000 in direct expenses alone, counting internal hours on resume review, engineering time pulled into interviews, and job board fees. A widely used industry benchmark puts the cost of a bad hire at 30% of first-year earnings, and SHRM estimates replacement costs


[between 50% and 200% of annual salary](https://www.shrm.org/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat) depending on the role.


When a role sits open, the rest of the team absorbs the workload. I talked to a candidate recently whose reason for leaving was exactly that. His company couldn't hire the people they needed, he was working 80-hour weeks, and he had a family. So now his employer has two open roles instead of one.


There’s also a cultural cost that hiring leaders underestimate. A role that stays open for four months sends a signal to the existing team. People start wondering whether the company is a good place to work, and they start looking. How a company hires is one of the clearest external signals of how it operates internally, and candidates and current employees are both paying attention.


## What to look for in a direct placement partner


Every recruiting firm will tell you they can run a direct placement search. The structural differences between how those firms operate are where the outcomes diverge.


### The same person should be talking to both sides


The most important question to ask a recruiting partner is whether the person managing the client relationship is also the person talking to the candidates. In many firms, those are separate roles. An account team sells the engagement, passes requirements to a recruiting team, and the recruiting team is incentivized to get profiles in front of the client as fast as possible. Information gets lost in that handoff, and so does judgment.


I run a full desk, which means I'm the one who sources a candidate, interviews them, presents them to the client, and stays involved through the offer. That structure gives me something most recruiters don't have: the ability to say no. I've sent a candidate through a first-round interview, talked to them afterward, and gone back to the client to pull the recommendation. Pulling a candidate costs me a placement fee in the short term. But clients remember the time you told them not to move forward, and that trust is what keeps the relationship going long after a single search closes.


### Specialization should show up as network depth


The other thing worth evaluating is how a recruiter's specialization translates in practice. I've spent eight years focused on DevOps and QA in the same regional markets. That means I know the candidates personally, I know who's referred whom, and I can verify someone's track record through relationships rather than only relying on a resume.


In a market where


[AI-generated applications](https://www.kellyservices.com/insights/ai-in-hr-practical-applications-common-mistakes-and-how-to-get-started-in-2026) have made credentials harder to trust, that verification through an established network is becoming the most valuable thing a specialized recruiter offers. A large majority of the placements my team makes come from people we've worked with before or people who were referred to us by someone we've placed in the past.


## Find the right permanent hire, faster


The hiring market is moving quickly, and direct placement works best when it's treated as a strategic decision rather than a default. That means scoping roles for growth is as important as scoping for coverage. It means building culture alignment into the interview process from the start. And it means working with recruiting partners who are close enough to both sides of the search to know when a candidate is the right fit and when to walk away.


At Kelly, the person evaluating your candidates is the same person who sourced and interviewed them. That closeness is what makes it possible to move fast without cutting corners on fit, and to pull a recommendation when the match isn't right.
